title: Logic, Sets & Proofs
description: Propositional logic and truth tables, equivalences, quantifiers, rules of inference, direct, contrapositive, contradiction and induction proofs, sets, functions, relations, partial orders and modular arithmetic.

cards.title: Which kind of sentence counts as a **proposition** in logic?
cards.body:
A declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both.

Questions, commands and open sentences like "$x + 1 = 5$" (truth depends on $x$) are **not** propositions.

Example: "$2 + 3 = 5$" is a (true) proposition; "Close the door" is not.
Key idea: a proposition has exactly one truth value.
cards.searchQuery: proposition definition propositional logic

cards.title: How many rows does a truth table have for a compound proposition with $4$ distinct variables?
cards.body:
16

Each variable is independently true or false, so $n$ variables give $2^n$ rows.

Example: $p, q, r$ give $2^3 = 8$ rows.
Tip: list rows in binary-counting order so none are missed or repeated.
cards.searchQuery: truth table number of rows 2^n variables

cards.title: When is the conjunction $p \land q$ true?
cards.body:
Exactly when **both** $p$ and $q$ are true.

If either one is false, the conjunction is false.

Example: $T \land F$ is $F$.
Key idea: $\land$ is "and".
cards.searchQuery: conjunction truth table logical and

cards.title: When is the inclusive disjunction $p \lor q$ false?
cards.body:
Only when **both** $p$ and $q$ are false.

It is true if at least one of them is true, including when both are.

Watch out: in logic $\lor$ is inclusive; the exclusive version is $p \oplus q$.
cards.searchQuery: disjunction truth table inclusive or

cards.title: When is the exclusive or $p \oplus q$ true?
cards.body:
Exactly when one of $p, q$ is true and the other is false.

Equivalently, $p \oplus q$ is true when $p$ and $q$ have **different** truth values.

Example: $T \oplus T$ is $F$, while $T \lor T$ is $T$.
cards.searchQuery: exclusive or XOR truth table

cards.title: In which single case is the conditional $p \to q$ false?
cards.body:
When $p$ is true and $q$ is false.

In the other three rows ($TT$, $FT$, $FF$) the conditional is true.

Example: "If you pass, I'll buy lunch" is broken only if you pass and I don't buy lunch.
Watch out: a false hypothesis never makes $p \to q$ false.
cards.searchQuery: conditional statement truth table false case

cards.title: Which expression using only $\neg$ and $\lor$ is equivalent to $p \to q$?
cards.body:
$\neg p \lor q$

Both are false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false.

Why: either the hypothesis fails ($\neg p$) or the conclusion holds ($q$).
Tip: rewrite conditionals this way before applying De Morgan's laws.
cards.searchQuery: implication equivalent not p or q

cards.title: If $p$ is false, what is the truth value of $p \to q$ (true or false)?
cards.body:
true

When the hypothesis is false, the conditional is **vacuously true**, whatever $q$ is.

Example: "If $1 = 2$, then $3 = 7$" is a true statement.
Watch out: this convention keeps $p \to q \equiv \neg p \lor q$ consistent.
cards.searchQuery: vacuous truth conditional false hypothesis

cards.title: What is the **converse** of $p \to q$?
cards.body:
$q \to p$

It swaps the hypothesis and the conclusion.

Example: the converse of "If it rains, the street is wet" is "If the street is wet, it rains".
Watch out: the converse is **not** equivalent to the original.
cards.searchQuery: converse of a conditional statement

cards.title: What is the **inverse** of $p \to q$?
cards.body:
$\neg p \to \neg q$

It negates both parts but keeps their order.

Why: the inverse is the contrapositive of the converse, so it is equivalent to the converse, not to the original.
cards.searchQuery: inverse of a conditional statement logic

cards.title: What is the **contrapositive** of $p \to q$?
cards.body:
$
eg q 	o 
eg p$

It is **logically equivalent** to $p 	o q$.

Why: $
eg q 	o 
eg p \equiv 
eg
eg q \lor 
eg p \equiv q \lor 
eg p \equiv 
eg p \lor q$.
Tip: when a direct proof of $p 	o q$ is awkward, prove the contrapositive instead.
cards.searchQuery: contrapositive logically equivalent conditional

cards.title: Is the converse $q \to p$ logically equivalent to $p \to q$?
cards.body:
No.

They differ when $p$ and $q$ have different truth values. With $p = F$, $q = T$: $p \to q$ is true but $q \to p$ is false.

Example: "Every square is a rectangle" is true, but its converse "every rectangle is a square" is false.
Watch out: assuming the converse is a classic exam error.
cards.searchQuery: converse not equivalent to conditional statement

cards.title: When is the biconditional $p \leftrightarrow q$ true?
cards.body:
When $p$ and $q$ have the **same** truth value.

It is true on $TT$ and $FF$, and false on $TF$ and $FT$.

Key idea: read it as "$p$ if and only if $q$".
cards.searchQuery: biconditional truth table if and only if

cards.title: Write $p \leftrightarrow q$ using two conditionals and a conjunction.
cards.body:
$(p \to q) \land (q \to p)$

Both directions must hold.

Why: the conjunction is true exactly when the two conditionals are both true, that is, when $p$ and $q$ agree.
Tip: to prove "$p$ iff $q$" you prove both conditionals.
cards.searchQuery: biconditional equivalent two conditionals

cards.title: How is "$p$ only if $q$" written symbolically?
cards.body:
$p \to q$

"Only if" introduces the necessary condition: if $p$ holds, then $q$ must hold.

Example: "You pass only if you study" means pass $\to$ study.
Watch out: it is **not** $q \to p$.
cards.searchQuery: p only if q translation conditional

cards.title: "$p$ is sufficient for $q$" translates to which conditional?
cards.body:
$p \to q$

Knowing $p$ is enough to guarantee $q$.

Example: being in Paris is sufficient for being in France.
Mnemonic: **S**ufficient goes at the **S**tart of the arrow.
cards.searchQuery: sufficient condition conditional statement logic

cards.title: "$p$ is necessary for $q$" translates to which conditional?
cards.body:
$q \to p$

If $q$ is true, then $p$ had to be true.

Example: being in France is necessary for being in Paris.
Watch out: the necessary condition is the conclusion of the arrow, not the hypothesis.
cards.searchQuery: necessary condition conditional statement logic

cards.title: What is a **tautology**?
cards.body:
A compound proposition that is true for every assignment of truth values to its variables.

Example: $p \lor \neg p$ is a tautology.

Key idea: its truth-table column is all $T$.
cards.searchQuery: tautology definition propositional logic

cards.title: What is a **contradiction** in propositional logic?
cards.body:
A compound proposition that is false for every assignment of truth values.

Example: $p \land \neg p$.

Why: the negation of a contradiction is a tautology.
cards.searchQuery: contradiction definition propositional logic

cards.title: State De Morgan's law for $\neg(p \land q)$.
cards.body:
$\neg(p \land q) \equiv \neg p \lor \neg q$

Negating an "and" gives an "or" of the negations.

Example: "not (tall and fast)" means "not tall or not fast".
Mnemonic: flip the connective, negate each piece.
cards.searchQuery: De Morgan's law negation of conjunction

cards.title: State De Morgan's law for $\neg(p \lor q)$.
cards.body:
$\neg(p \lor q) \equiv \neg p \land \neg q$

Negating an "or" gives an "and" of the negations.

Example: "not (rain or snow)" means "no rain and no snow".
Watch out: forgetting to flip $\lor$ to $\land$ is the usual slip.
cards.searchQuery: De Morgan's law negation of disjunction

cards.title: What is $\neg(p \to q)$ equivalent to?
cards.body:
$p \land 
eg q$

A conditional fails only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false.

Why: $
eg(
eg p \lor q) \equiv 
eg
eg p \land 
eg q \equiv p \land 
eg q$.
Watch out: the negation of a conditional is **not** another conditional.
cards.searchQuery: negation of implication equivalent p and not q

cards.title: Distribute: $p \land (q \lor r) \equiv\,?$
cards.body:
$(p \land q) \lor (p \land r)$

$\land$ distributes over $\lor$, and likewise $\lor$ distributes over $\land$: $p \lor (q \land r) \equiv (p \lor q) \land (p \lor r)$.

Tip: both distributive laws hold, unlike ordinary arithmetic where only multiplication distributes over addition.
cards.searchQuery: distributive laws propositional logic

cards.title: Simplify $p \lor (p \land q)$.
cards.body:
$p$

This is an **absorption law**; the dual is $p \land (p \lor q) \equiv p$.

Why: if $p$ is true the whole thing is true; if $p$ is false, then $p \land q$ is false too, so the result is false.
cards.searchQuery: absorption law logic p or p and q

cards.title: What is the name of the law $p \lor \neg p \equiv \mathbf{T}$?
cards.body:
law of excluded middle

Every proposition is either true or its negation is true.

The companion law $p \land \neg p \equiv \mathbf{F}$ is the law of **non-contradiction**.
cards.searchQuery: law of excluded middle propositional logic

cards.title: In how many of the $4$ rows of its truth table is $p \to q$ true?
cards.body:
3

The conditional is false only on the row $p = T$, $q = F$.

Key idea: a conditional is true in most rows, so it is a weak statement compared with $p \land q$ (true in $1$ row).
cards.searchQuery: conditional truth table three true rows

cards.title: Among the $16$ truth assignments to $p, q, r, s$, how many make $p \to q$ false?
cards.body:
4

$p \to q$ is false only when $p = T$ and $q = F$.

The other two variables $r$ and $s$ are free: $2 \times 2 = 4$ assignments.
Tip: fix the variables that decide the outcome, then multiply by $2$ for each free one.
cards.searchQuery: count truth assignments conditional false free variables

cards.title: Which statement is equivalent to $(p \land q) \to r$?
cards.body:
$p 	o (q 	o r)$

This is the **exportation** law: move a conjunct from the hypothesis into a nested conditional.

Why: $
eg(p \land q) \lor r \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q \lor r \equiv 
eg p \lor (
eg q \lor r)$.
cards.searchQuery: exportation law logic equivalence conditional

cards.title: Is $\to$ associative, that is, $(p \to q) \to r \equiv p \to (q \to r)$?
cards.body:
No.

Take $p = q = r = F$. Then $(F \to F) \to F = T \to F = F$, but $F \to (F \to F) = F \to T = T$.

Watch out: always parenthesize chained conditionals; $\land$ and $\lor$ are associative, $\to$ is not.
cards.searchQuery: implication not associative counterexample logic

cards.title: Let $p = T$ and $q = F$. What is the truth value of $(p \lor q) \to \neg p$ (true or false)?
cards.body:
false

Here $p \lor q = T$ and $\neg p = F$, so the conditional is $T \to F$, which is false.

Tip: evaluate the innermost parts first, then work outward.
cards.searchQuery: evaluate compound proposition truth value conditional

cards.title: What does $\forall x\, P(x)$ assert?
cards.body:
$P(x)$ is true for **every** $x$ in the domain.

It is false as soon as one element makes $P$ false.

Example: $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ (x^2 \ge 0)$ is true.
Watch out: the truth of a quantified statement depends on the domain.
cards.searchQuery: universal quantifier for all meaning

cards.title: What does $\exists x\, P(x)$ assert?
cards.body:
There is **at least one** $x$ in the domain for which $P(x)$ is true.

One witness is enough to prove it.

Example: $\exists x \in \mathbb{Z}\ (x^2 = 9)$ is true, witnessed by $x = 3$.
cards.searchQuery: existential quantifier there exists meaning

cards.title: What is $\neg\,\forall x\, P(x)$ equivalent to?
cards.body:
$\exists x\, \neg P(x)$

"Not everything has the property" means "something lacks it".

Example: "Not every bird flies" is "some bird does not fly".
Mnemonic: push the $\neg$ inside and swap the quantifier.
cards.searchQuery: negation of universal quantifier equivalent exists not

cards.title: What is $\neg\,\exists x\, P(x)$ equivalent to?
cards.body:
$\forall x\, \neg P(x)$

"There is no $x$ with the property" means "every $x$ lacks it".

Example: "No integer satisfies $x^2 = 2$" is "for all integers, $x^2 \ne 2$".
cards.searchQuery: negation of existential quantifier equivalent for all not

cards.title: Over the integers, which of $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x + y = 0)$ and $\exists y\,\forall x\,(x + y = 0)$ is true?
cards.body:
Only the first one: $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x + y = 0)$.

In the first, $y$ may depend on $x$ (take $y = -x$). In the second, one fixed $y$ would have to work for every $x$, which is impossible.

Watch out: swapping $\forall$ and $\exists$ changes the meaning.
cards.searchQuery: order of quantifiers for all there exists matters

cards.title: Over an **empty** domain, what are the truth values of $\forall x\, P(x)$ and $\exists x\, P(x)$?
cards.body:
$\forall x\, P(x)$ is true (vacuously); $\exists x\, P(x)$ is false.

There is no element to violate $P$, and no element to witness it.

Example: "Every unicorn in this room is purple" is vacuously true if the room has no unicorns.
cards.searchQuery: empty domain universal quantifier vacuously true

cards.title: Which formula says "every $A$ is a $B$"?
cards.body:
$\forall x\,(A(x) \to B(x))$

The universal quantifier pairs with a **conditional**.

Watch out: $\forall x\,(A(x) \land B(x))$ would claim that *everything* is both $A$ and $B$.
cards.searchQuery: translate all A are B universal quantifier conditional

cards.title: Which formula says "some $A$ is a $B$"?
cards.body:
$\exists x\,(A(x) \land B(x))$

The existential quantifier pairs with a **conjunction**.

Watch out: $\exists x\,(A(x) \to B(x))$ is far too weak; it is true whenever some element is not an $A$.
cards.searchQuery: translate some A are B existential quantifier conjunction

cards.title: How do you disprove a statement of the form $\forall x\, P(x)$?
cards.body:
Exhibit a single **counterexample**: one $x$ in the domain with $P(x)$ false.

This works because $\neg\forall x\, P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \neg P(x)$.

Example: "every prime is odd" fails at $x = 2$.
Watch out: examples never prove a universal claim; one counterexample always disproves it.
cards.searchQuery: counterexample disprove universal statement

cards.title: Does $\forall x\,(P(x) \lor Q(x))$ imply $\forall x\,P(x) \lor \forall x\,Q(x)$?
cards.body:
No.

Over the integers let $P(x)$ be "$x$ is even" and $Q(x)$ be "$x$ is odd". Every integer is even or odd, but not all are even and not all are odd.

Key idea: $\forall$ distributes over $\land$, but not over $\lor$.
cards.searchQuery: universal quantifier distribute over disjunction counterexample

cards.title: Name the rule of inference: from $p \to q$ and $p$, conclude $q$.
cards.body:
modus ponens

The tautology behind it is $(p \land (p \to q)) \to q$.

Example: "If it rains, the ground is wet. It rains. So the ground is wet."
cards.searchQuery: modus ponens rule of inference

cards.title: Name the rule of inference: from $p \to q$ and $\neg q$, conclude $\neg p$.
cards.body:
modus tollens

The tautology behind it is $(\neg q \land (p \to q)) \to \neg p$.

Example: "If it rained, the ground is wet. The ground is dry. So it did not rain."
Why: it is modus ponens applied to the contrapositive $\neg q \to \neg p$.
cards.searchQuery: modus tollens rule of inference

cards.title: What does the **hypothetical syllogism** rule conclude from $p \to q$ and $q \to r$?
cards.body:
$p \to r$

Conditionals chain together.

Example: "If I study, I learn. If I learn, I pass." So "if I study, I pass".
cards.searchQuery: hypothetical syllogism rule of inference

cards.title: What does the **disjunctive syllogism** rule conclude from $p \lor q$ and $\neg p$?
cards.body:
$q$

If one of two options is ruled out, the other must hold.

Example: "The answer is $3$ or $5$. It is not $3$. So it is $5$."
cards.searchQuery: disjunctive syllogism rule of inference

cards.title: Why is "$p \to q$ and $q$, therefore $p$" an invalid argument?
cards.body:
It **affirms the conclusion** (the fallacy of the converse).

With $p = F$ and $q = T$, both premises are true but $p$ is false.

Example: "If it rains, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained." (A hose could have done it.)
cards.searchQuery: fallacy of affirming the conclusion

cards.title: Why is "$p \to q$ and $\neg p$, therefore $\neg q$" an invalid argument?
cards.body:
It **denies the hypothesis** (the fallacy of the inverse).

With $p = F$ and $q = T$, both premises are true but $\neg q$ is false.

Watch out: this looks like modus tollens, but modus tollens negates the conclusion, not the hypothesis.
cards.searchQuery: fallacy of denying the hypothesis

cards.title: What does the **resolution** rule conclude from $p \lor q$ and $\neg p \lor r$?
cards.body:
$q \lor r$

One of $p, \neg p$ is false, so the clause containing it forces the other literal.

Why: if $p$ is true then $r$ holds; if $p$ is false then $q$ holds.
Key idea: resolution is the engine of SAT solvers and automated theorem provers.
cards.searchQuery: resolution rule of inference clauses

cards.title: What does **universal instantiation** allow you to conclude from $\forall x\, P(x)$?
cards.body:
$P(c)$ for any particular element $c$ of the domain.

Example: from "all humans are mortal" infer "Socrates is mortal".

Watch out: the reverse step, universal **generalization**, is only valid when $c$ was an arbitrary element, not a special one.
cards.searchQuery: universal instantiation universal generalization rules

cards.title: How does a **direct proof** of $p \to q$ proceed?
cards.body:
Assume $p$ is true, then reason step by step until you reach $q$.

Example: if $n$ is odd, write $n = 2k + 1$; then $n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$ is odd.
Tip: start by unpacking the definitions in the hypothesis.
cards.searchQuery: direct proof method assume hypothesis

cards.title: How does a proof by **contrapositive** of $p \to q$ proceed?
cards.body:
Assume $\neg q$ and show $\neg p$.

Since $\neg q \to \neg p$ is equivalent to $p \to q$, this proves the original statement.

Tip: use it when the conclusion $q$ is easier to negate than the hypothesis is to exploit, such as "$n$ is even".
cards.searchQuery: proof by contrapositive method

cards.title: How does a proof by **contradiction** of a statement $p$ proceed?
cards.body:
Assume $\neg p$ and derive a contradiction (some statement and its negation).

Then $\neg p$ is impossible, so $p$ is true.

Watch out: to prove $p \to q$ this way, assume $p \land \neg q$, not just $\neg q$.
cards.searchQuery: proof by contradiction method

cards.title: Using the contrapositive, how do you prove: if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even?
cards.body:
Prove: if $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd.

Write $n = 2k + 1$. Then $n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$, which is odd.

Why: a direct attack starting from $n^2 = 2m$ gives no easy way to extract $n$.
Key idea: this lemma drives the proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
cards.searchQuery: if n squared is even then n is even proof contrapositive

cards.title: In the classic contradiction proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, what do you assume and what contradiction do you reach?
cards.body:
Assume $\sqrt{2} = a/b$ in lowest terms; you reach "$a$ and $b$ are both even".

From $a^2 = 2b^2$, $a^2$ is even, so $a$ is even. Write $a = 2c$; then $b^2 = 2c^2$, so $b$ is even too.

Both even contradicts lowest terms, so $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
cards.searchQuery: proof square root of 2 irrational contradiction

cards.title: In Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes, what number is built from the assumed finite list $p_1, \dots, p_k$?
cards.body:
$N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1$

$N > 1$, so it has a prime divisor. But dividing $N$ by any $p_i$ leaves remainder $1$, so that prime is not on the list: contradiction.

Watch out: $N$ itself need not be prime; the proof only needs a prime **divisor** of $N$.
cards.searchQuery: Euclid proof infinitely many primes p1 pk plus 1

cards.title: What are the two steps of **mathematical induction** for proving $P(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$?
cards.body:
Base case: show $P(n_0)$. Inductive step: show $P(k) \to P(k+1)$ for every $k \ge n_0$.

Together they give $P(n_0), P(n_0+1), \dots$ like falling dominoes.

Watch out: the assumption $P(k)$ is the **inductive hypothesis**; assuming it is not circular because you only prove $P(k+1)$ from it.
cards.searchQuery: mathematical induction base case inductive step

cards.title: Using $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ (provable by induction), what is $1 + 2 + \cdots + 100$?
cards.body:
5050

$\dfrac{100 \cdot 101}{2} = 5050$.

Why: inductive step: $\dfrac{k(k+1)}{2} + (k+1) = \dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$.
Example: $n = 4$ gives $1+2+3+4 = 10 = \dfrac{4 \cdot 5}{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: sum of first n integers induction proof formula

cards.title: How does **strong induction** differ from ordinary induction in its inductive step?
cards.body:
It assumes $P(j)$ is true for **all** $j$ with $n_0 \le j \le k$, not just $P(k)$, and proves $P(k+1)$.

The two forms are equivalent in power, but strong induction is more convenient when $P(k+1)$ depends on several earlier cases.

Example: every integer $n \ge 2$ is a product of primes; the factors of $n$ may be much smaller than $n - 1$.
cards.searchQuery: strong induction versus weak induction

cards.title: In the false induction "proof" that all horses have the same color, which step actually fails?
cards.body:
The inductive step from $k = 1$ to $k = 2$.

The argument splits a group into two overlapping sets of $k$ horses, but when $k + 1 = 2$ the two sets share no horse, so the colors are never linked.

Key idea: an inductive step must work for **every** $k \ge$ the base case, including the first one.
cards.searchQuery: all horses same color induction fallacy

cards.title: State the **well-ordering principle**.
cards.body:
Every nonempty set of nonnegative integers has a least element.

It is equivalent to mathematical induction and is often used to argue by a "smallest counterexample".

Watch out: it fails for the nonnegative reals or rationals, where sets like $\{x : x > 0\}$ have no least element.
cards.searchQuery: well-ordering principle nonnegative integers least element

cards.title: What is the difference between a constructive and a nonconstructive existence proof?
cards.body:
A constructive proof **exhibits** the object; a nonconstructive proof shows it must exist without producing it.

Example: to show irrational $a, b$ exist with $a^b$ rational, take $a = b = \sqrt{2}$ if $\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ is rational. Otherwise take $a = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$, $b = \sqrt{2}$, giving $a^b = 2$.

That proof never says which case holds.
cards.searchQuery: constructive versus nonconstructive existence proof

cards.title: The sum of the first $n$ odd positive integers is $n^2$ (provable by induction). What is $1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + 19$ (the first $10$ odd numbers)?
cards.body:
100

The sum is $10^2 = 100$.

Why: inductive step: $k^2 + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)^2$.
Tip: the $n$th odd number is $2n - 1$, so $19$ is the $10$th.
cards.searchQuery: sum of first n odd numbers equals n squared induction

cards.title: Using $\sum_{i=0}^{n} 2^i = 2^{n+1} - 1$ (provable by induction), what is $1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 128$?
cards.searchQuery: geometric series powers of 2 sum induction 2^(n+1) - 1

cards.title: What is $|\{1, 2, 2, 3\}|$?
cards.body:
3

A set ignores repeated elements and order, so $\{1, 2, 2, 3\} = \{1, 2, 3\}$.

Watch out: $|A|$ counts distinct elements only.
cards.searchQuery: set cardinality duplicates ignored distinct elements

cards.title: Is the empty set $\emptyset$ a subset of every set?
cards.body:
Yes: $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for every set $A$.

Why: $\forall x\,(x \in \emptyset \to x \in A)$ is vacuously true because $x \in \emptyset$ is always false.

Watch out: $\emptyset \subseteq A$ is always true, but $\emptyset \in A$ only if $\emptyset$ is listed as an element.
cards.searchQuery: empty set subset of every set vacuous proof

cards.title: What is $|\{\emptyset\}|$?
cards.body:
1

$\{\emptyset\}$ is a set with exactly one element, namely the empty set.

Watch out: $|\emptyset| = 0$, but $\{\emptyset\}$ is not empty; it is a box containing an empty box.
cards.searchQuery: cardinality of set containing empty set

cards.title: A set $A$ has $5$ elements. How many elements does its power set $\mathcal{P}(A)$ have?
cards.body:
32

$|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|} = 2^5 = 32$.

Why: each element is either in or out of a subset, giving $2$ choices per element.
Example: $\mathcal{P}(\{a, b\}) = \{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a, b\}\}$ has $4$ elements.
cards.searchQuery: power set cardinality 2^n subsets

cards.title: If $|A| = 3$ and $|B| = 4$, what is $|A \times B|$?
cards.body:
12

$|A \times B| = |A| \cdot |B|$, since $A \times B$ is the set of ordered pairs $(a, b)$.

Example: $\{1, 2\} \times \{x\} = \{(1, x), (2, x)\}$.
Watch out: $A \times B \ne B \times A$ in general, because pairs are ordered.
cards.searchQuery: cartesian product cardinality ordered pairs

cards.title: Define the set difference $A \setminus B$.
cards.body:
$A \setminus B = \{x : x \in A \land x \notin B\}$

The elements of $A$ that are not in $B$.

Example: $\{1, 2, 3\} \setminus \{2, 5\} = \{1, 3\}$.
Watch out: $A \setminus B \ne B \setminus A$ in general.
cards.searchQuery: set difference definition A minus B

cards.title: What is the symmetric difference $\{1, 2, 3\} \oplus \{3, 4\}$?
cards.body:
$\{1, 2, 4\}$

$A \oplus B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)$: elements in exactly one of the two sets.

Key idea: it is the set analogue of exclusive or.
cards.searchQuery: symmetric difference of sets definition example

cards.title: State De Morgan's law for the complement of $A \cap B$.
cards.body:
$\overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}$

The dual law is $\overline{A \cup B} = \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}$.

Why: $x 
otin A \cap B$ means $x 
otin A$ or $x 
otin B$, the set form of $
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q$.
cards.searchQuery: De Morgan's laws sets complement of intersection

cards.title: How do you prove $A \subseteq B$ directly?
cards.body:
Take an **arbitrary** $x \in A$ and show that $x \in B$.

This proves $\forall x\,(x \in A \to x \in B)$.

Example: to show $A \cap B \subseteq A$, let $x \in A \cap B$; then $x \in A$ and $x \in B$, so $x \in A$.
Watch out: do not pick a specific $x$; that would not cover all of $A$.
cards.searchQuery: how to prove a set is a subset arbitrary element

cards.title: How do you prove two sets are equal, $A = B$, by an element argument?
cards.body:
Show both inclusions: $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$.

This is the set version of proving a biconditional by proving both conditionals.

Tip: when a chain of "iff" steps with set-builder membership works, it proves both inclusions at once.
cards.searchQuery: prove set equality double inclusion

cards.title: What conditions make a relation from $A$ to $B$ a **function** $f : A \to B$?
cards.body:
Every element of $A$ is assigned **exactly one** element of $B$.

So each input has an output, and never two different outputs.

Example: $x \mapsto \pm\sqrt{x}$ is not a function, because $4$ would have two outputs.
Key idea: $A$ is the domain and $B$ is the codomain.
cards.searchQuery: function definition domain codomain exactly one output

cards.title: What does it mean for $f : A \to B$ to be **injective** (one-to-one)?
cards.body:
Different inputs give different outputs: $f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b$.

Example: $f(x) = 2x + 1$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is injective; $f(x) = x^2$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is not, since $f(-1) = f(1)$.
Tip: to prove injectivity, assume $f(a) = f(b)$ and deduce $a = b$.
cards.searchQuery: injective function definition one-to-one

cards.title: What does it mean for $f : A \to B$ to be **surjective** (onto)?
cards.body:
Every element of the codomain is hit: for every $b \in B$ there is some $a \in A$ with $f(a) = b$.

Example: $f(x) = 2x$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ is not onto, because odd numbers are never reached.
Key idea: surjective means range = codomain.
cards.searchQuery: surjective function definition onto codomain

cards.title: When does a function $f : A \to B$ have an inverse function $f^{-1} : B \to A$?
cards.body:
Exactly when $f$ is a **bijection** (both injective and surjective).

Injective makes each output come from one input; surjective makes sure every element of $B$ has one.

Watch out: $f^{-1}$ means the inverse function, not $1/f$.
cards.searchQuery: bijection inverse function exists injective surjective

cards.title: How many functions are there from a $3$-element set to a $2$-element set?
cards.body:
8

Each of the $3$ inputs independently picks one of $2$ outputs: $2^3 = 8$.

Key idea: there are $|B|^{|A|}$ functions from $A$ to $B$.
Watch out: do not swap the base and exponent; $3^2 = 9$ counts functions the other way.
cards.searchQuery: number of functions from A to B |B|^|A|

cards.title: How many bijections are there from a $4$-element set to itself?
cards.body:
24

Choose images one input at a time: $4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 4! = 24$.

Key idea: bijections between two $n$-element sets number $n!$.
cards.searchQuery: number of bijections n factorial permutations

cards.title: Let $f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$. What is $(f \circ g)(3)$?
cards.body:
19

$(f \circ g)(3) = f(g(3)) = f(9) = 2 \cdot 9 + 1 = 19$.

Watch out: apply $g$ first. The other order gives $(g \circ f)(3) = g(7) = 49$.
cards.searchQuery: function composition f of g evaluate order

cards.title: What is $\lfloor -2.5 \rfloor$?
cards.body:
-3

The floor is the **greatest integer less than or equal to** the number, and $-3 \le -2.5 < -2$.

Watch out: floor does not just drop the decimal part for negatives. $\lceil -2.5 \rceil = -2$.
cards.searchQuery: floor function negative number -2.5 greatest integer

cards.title: What is a **binary relation** from a set $A$ to a set $B$?
cards.body:
Any subset $R \subseteq A \times B$ of ordered pairs.

We write $a \mathrel{R} b$ when $(a, b) \in R$. A relation **on** $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$.

Example: "$<$" on $\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of pairs $(a, b)$ with $a < b$.
cards.searchQuery: binary relation definition subset of cartesian product

cards.title: What does it mean for a relation $R$ on $A$ to be **reflexive**?
cards.body:
$(a, a) \in R$ for every $a \in A$.

Example: $\le$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is reflexive; $<$ is not.

Watch out: a single $a$ with $(a, a) \notin R$ breaks reflexivity.
cards.searchQuery: reflexive relation definition example

cards.title: What does it mean for a relation $R$ on $A$ to be **transitive**?
cards.body:
Whenever $(a, b) \in R$ and $(b, c) \in R$, then $(a, c) \in R$.

Example: $<$ and "divides" are transitive; "is a parent of" is not (a grandparent is not a parent).
Tip: to disprove it, find $a, b, c$ with $a \mathrel{R} b$, $b \mathrel{R} c$ but not $a \mathrel{R} c$.
cards.searchQuery: transitive relation definition example

cards.title: What does it mean for a relation $R$ on $A$ to be **antisymmetric**?
cards.body:
If $(a, b) \in R$ and $(b, a) \in R$, then $a = b$.

Example: $\le$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is antisymmetric but not symmetric.

Watch out: antisymmetric is **not** the opposite of symmetric. Equality is both, and some relations are neither.
cards.searchQuery: antisymmetric relation definition vs symmetric

cards.title: What three properties make a relation an **equivalence relation**?
cards.body:
Reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

Example: congruence modulo $n$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is an equivalence relation.

Key idea: equivalence relations formalize "having the same ___", such as the same remainder.
cards.searchQuery: equivalence relation reflexive symmetric transitive

cards.title: How do the equivalence classes of an equivalence relation on $A$ divide up $A$?
cards.body:
They form a **partition**: every element lies in exactly one class, and any two classes are either equal or disjoint.

Example: congruence mod $3$ splits $\mathbb{Z}$ into the classes of remainders $0$, $1$ and $2$.
Key idea: $[a] = [b]$ exactly when $a \mathrel{R} b$.
cards.searchQuery: equivalence classes partition set

cards.title: How many binary relations are there on a $3$-element set?
cards.body:
512

A relation is any subset of $A \times A$, which has $3^2 = 9$ pairs, so there are $2^9 = 512$ subsets.

Key idea: on an $n$-element set there are $2^{n^2}$ relations.
cards.searchQuery: number of binary relations on a set 2^(n^2)

cards.title: What three properties make a relation a **partial order**?
cards.body:
Reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.

Example: $\le$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, $\subseteq$ on a family of sets, and divisibility on positive integers.

Key idea: a set with a partial order is called a **poset**.
cards.searchQuery: partial order definition reflexive antisymmetric transitive poset

cards.title: When is a partial order a **total order**?
cards.body:
When every two elements $a, b$ are comparable: $a \preceq b$ or $b \preceq a$.

Example: $\le$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is total. $\subseteq$ on subsets of $\{1, 2\}$ is not, because $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are incomparable.
cards.searchQuery: total order definition comparable elements

cards.title: Is divisibility ($a \mid b$) on the positive integers a total order?
cards.body:
No, it is only a partial order.

For example, $2 \nmid 3$ and $3 \nmid 2$, so $2$ and $3$ are incomparable.

Why: it is reflexive ($a \mid a$), antisymmetric (on positive integers $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$ force $a = b$) and transitive.
cards.searchQuery: divisibility partial order not total incomparable

cards.title: What is left out when you draw a **Hasse diagram** of a finite poset?
cards.body:
Loops and edges implied by transitivity; arrows are replaced by upward direction.

Only the "covering" relations $a \prec b$ (nothing strictly between) are drawn, with $a$ below $b$.

Example: in divisibility on $\{1, 2, 4\}$ you draw $1$-$2$ and $2$-$4$ but not $1$-$4$.
cards.searchQuery: Hasse diagram poset covering relation transitivity omitted

cards.title: What is the difference between a **maximal** element and a **greatest** element of a poset?
cards.body:
Maximal: nothing is strictly above it. Greatest: it is above (or equal to) every element.

Example: under divisibility on $\{2, 3, 4, 6\}$, both $4$ and $6$ are maximal, but there is no greatest element.

Key idea: a greatest element is maximal, but a maximal element need not be greatest.
cards.searchQuery: maximal element versus greatest element poset

cards.title: What does $a \equiv b \pmod{n}$ mean?
cards.body:
$n$ divides $a - b$, so $a$ and $b$ leave the same remainder on division by $n$.

Example: $17 \equiv 2 \pmod{5}$ because $5 \mid 15$.

Watch out: $\equiv$ is a relation between integers; "$a \bmod n$" denotes the remainder, a single value in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
cards.searchQuery: congruence modulo n definition divides a minus b

cards.title: If $a \equiv b$ and $c \equiv d \pmod{n}$, what can you say about $a + c$ and $ac$?
cards.body:
$a + c \equiv b + d$ and $ac \equiv bd \pmod{n}$.

So you can reduce numbers mod $n$ at any step of a sum or product.

Example: $(14 \cdot 23) \bmod 5 = (4 \cdot 3) \bmod 5 = 2$.
Watch out: you cannot cancel a common factor in general. $2 \cdot 1 \equiv 2 \cdot 4 \pmod 6$, but $1 \not\equiv 4$.
cards.searchQuery: modular arithmetic addition multiplication congruence properties

cards.title: What is $-7 \bmod 5$ (the remainder in $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$)?
cards.body:
3

$-7 = (-2)\cdot 5 + 3$, and the remainder must be nonnegative and less than $5$.

Watch out: many programming languages return $-2$ for `-7 % 5`; in discrete math the remainder is never negative.
cards.searchQuery: negative number modulo remainder -7 mod 5

cards.title: What is $\gcd(48, 18)$?
cards.body:
6

The Euclidean algorithm: $\gcd(48, 18) = \gcd(18, 12) = \gcd(12, 6) = \gcd(6, 0) = 6$.

Tip: check by prime factorization: $48 = 2^4 \cdot 3$ and $18 = 2 \cdot 3^2$, so the gcd is $2 \cdot 3 = 6$.
cards.searchQuery: gcd of 48 and 18 Euclidean algorithm

cards.title: What identity powers the Euclidean algorithm for $\gcd(a, b)$ with $b > 0$?
cards.body:
$\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b,\ a \bmod b)$

Repeat until the remainder is $0$; the last nonzero remainder is the gcd.

Why: any common divisor of $a$ and $b$ also divides $a - qb = a \bmod b$, and vice versa.
cards.searchQuery: Euclidean algorithm gcd a b equals gcd b a mod b

cards.title: What does **Bezout's identity** say about $\gcd(a, b)$?
cards.body:
There exist integers $s, t$ with $\gcd(a, b) = sa + tb$.

Example: $6 = \gcd(48, 18) = (-1)\cdot 48 + 3 \cdot 18$.

Key idea: the extended Euclidean algorithm finds $s$ and $t$; this is how modular inverses are computed.
cards.searchQuery: Bezout's identity gcd linear combination

cards.title: What is the inverse of $3$ modulo $7$, as a number in $\{1, \dots, 6\}$?
cards.body:
5

$3 \cdot 5 = 15 = 2 \cdot 7 + 1$, so $3 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$.

Key idea: $a$ has an inverse mod $n$ exactly when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.
cards.searchQuery: modular inverse of 3 mod 7 gcd 1

cards.title: Compute $3^{100} \bmod 7$.
cards.body:
4

Fermat's little theorem: $3^6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$. Since $100 = 6 \cdot 16 + 4$, $3^{100} \equiv 3^4 = 81 \equiv 4$.

Key idea: for prime $p$ and $p \nmid a$, $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$, so exponents reduce mod $p - 1$.
cards.searchQuery: Fermat's little theorem 3^100 mod 7
